agree.reason: The sales record, reading-list printing, $12,500 comparable and free extras give a well-disposed editor real grounds to go above $9,000, but nothing explains why Elena is worth $3,500 more than the $8,000 newcomer, so the editor could easily settle on a counter in the $10,000s.

honest.reason: It rightly drops the unsupported claim that 'every other publisher pays at least $12,000', but it states the agent's $11,000–$13,000 range as 'the standard rate' instead of crediting the agent, which presents an opinion as market fact.

works_the_facts.reason: The facts are accurate but not worked: it never says the fee has stayed flat across six books and four years, that $11,500 is still $1,000 below what another publisher paid last year, or what $9,000 comes to for four months of work.

right_comparison.reason: It compares the fee with the outside market but not with the editor's real alternative, an untested illustrator, against Elena's proven 20,000-copy sellers, and it only hints at the trend of a rising record against a fixed fee.

qualification.reason: The commitments are concrete and checkable (sketches within six weeks of signing, final art by September 1, two spot drawings, an answer by the end of next week), but there's no real conditional, and it doesn't spell out what happens at a figure between $9,000 and $11,500.

objections.reason: The extras and firm deadlines partly answer budget worries, but the email never takes on the main objections, the $9,000 budget limit and the cheaper newer illustrator, for example by pointing to the lower risk of an illustrator with a proven sales record.

fit.reason: It's a polite, well-ordered email of about 200 words with a subject line, so it's within the 250-word limit and matches the form requested.
